1.
An information that a lady has committed suicide was received in the police station R K Puram through DD No.14A on 12.10.2008, which brought the police machinery into action.

SI Rajesh Kumar, who was deputed to the spot found that deceased Nutan was married barely a year ago and,
therefore, he ensured that the parents of the deceased were informed.
He got the site inspected through the crime team, which was called at the spot.

The body was removed to the hospital and needful was got done.
2. On 14.10.2008 father of the deceased namely Upender Kumar Jha came to Delhi and gave his statement to the Executive Magistrate whereby he informed that deceased Nutan was married to Amod Kumar Mishra on 22.02.2008 with the consent of both the families.

The usual ceremonies were performed in respect to the marriage, however, he alleged that Nutan was being tortured and State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 2 of 29 harassed for various reasons, primarily belonging to rural background and for not bringing enough dowry.

entities.text: State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors

sentences.text: The harassment gradually exceeded from verbal assault to physical assault.
He had even transmitted a sum of Rs.75,000/ in three installments of Rs. 30,000/, 20,000/ and 25,000/ to meet the demand and in order to make the life of his daughter Nutan comfortable.
The harassment and torture, however, continued and the deceased Nutan confided about this to her sister, who too was living in Delhi and other family members.

Father of the deceased conveyed to the authorities that his daughter Nutan was killed by her husband, his brother i.e. Amod Kumar and Pramod Kumar respectively, Sunita, sisterinlaw and Taruna Devi, motherinlaw of the deceased, as it was the harassment and torture perpetuated by them which drove Nutan to commit suicide.
Based upon such statement an FIR was registered.
Kashinath Jha (Mausa of Amod Mishra and Pramod Mishra) was also blamed and thereafter he too was arraigned in the list of accused persons.

The investigation ultimately culminated into the chargesheet filed under section 304B/498A/34 IPC.
3.
After compliance of section 207 Cr.P.C., the case was committed to the Court of Sessions.

Based upon the allegations and the investigation carried out, prima facie case under section State Vs.
Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 3 of 29 304B/498/34 IPC was found against the aforesaid five accused persons i.e. Amod Mishra, Pramod Mishra, Arti, Taruna and Kashinath Jha and accordingly a charge was framed qua all of them, to which they pleaded not guilty.

sentences.text: (a) any willful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to life, limb or health (whether mental or physical) of the woman; or (b) harassment of the woman where such harassment is with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet any unlawful demand for any property or valuable security or is on account of failure by her or any person related to her to meet such demand.

Expression 'soon before her death': meaning of "The expression 'soon before her death' used in the substantive section 304B, IPC and section 113B of the Evidence Act is State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 9 of 29 present with the idea of proximity text.

entities.text: State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 9 of 29

sentences.text: No definite period has been indicated and the expression 'soon before her death' is not defined.
The determination of the period which can come within the term 'soon before her death' is left to be determined by the courts, depending upon facts and circumstances of each case.
Suffice, however, to indicate that the expression 'soon before would normally imply that the interval should not be much between the concerned cruelty or harassment and the death in question.
There must be existence of a proximate and livelink between the effect of cruelty based on dowry demand and the concerned death.

If alleged incident of cruelty is remote in time and has become stale enough not to disturb mental equilibrium of the woman concerned, it would be of no consequence".

The evidence brought on record is required to be tested on the aforesaid parameters in order to ascertain as to whether the prosecution is able to establish its case or not.
The prosecution has primarily relied upon the testimony of the father, brother and sister of the deceased examined as PW3, PW4 and PW5.

Certain aspects of the matter do not require any evidence in view of the fact that there is no dispute about the date of marriage of the deceased State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 10 of 29 Nutan and Amod Mishra which took place on 22.02.2008 and that she expired / died on 10.12.2008.

17. The judgment in State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal and anr., : (1994) 1 SCC 73 can be looked into where the following observations were made by the Hon'ble Apex Court:
We are not oblivious that in a criminal trial the degree of proof is stricter than what is required in a civil proceedings.

entities.text: State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal and anr., : (1994) 1 SCC 73
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In a criminal trial however intriguing may be facts and circumstances of the case, the charges made against the accused must be proved beyond all reasonable doubts and the requirement of proof cannot lie in the realm of surmises and conjectures.

The requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not stand altered even after the introduction of section 498A IPC and section 113A of the Indian State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 13 of 29 Evidence Act.

entities.text: Indian State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 13 of 29
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Although, the Court's conscience must be satisfied that the accused is not held guilty when there are reasonable doubts about the complicity of the accused in respect of the offences alleged, it should be borne in mind that there is no absolute standard for proof in a criminal trial and the question whether the charges made against the accused have been proved beyond all reasonable doubts must depend upon the facts and circumstances of the case and the quality of the evidence adduced in the case and the materials placed on record.

Lord Denning in Bater Vs. Bater, 1950 (2) AII ER 458, 459 has observed that the doubt must of a reasonable man and the standard adopted be a standard adopted by a reasonable and just man for coming to a conclusion considering the particular subject matter.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Reference in this context can be made to the judgment in Kaliyaperumal v. State of Tamil Nadu, AIR 2003 SC 3828."
The evidence brought on record is required to be tested on the aforesaid parameters in order to ascertain as to whether the prosecution is able to establish its case or not.
Certain aspects of the matter do not require any evidence in view of the fact that there is no dispute about the date of marriage of the deceased State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 10 of 29 Nutan and Amod Mishra which took place on 22.02.2008 and that she expired / died on 10.12.2008.
Evidently the death is within seven years of marriage giving rise to the presumption against the accused persons under section 113B of the Indian Evidence Act.
However,
the presumption is, as all presumptions are, rebuttable, so is this.
Thus ,two aspects are to be seen as to whether the prosecution has been able to establish its case and the ingredients above referred and as to whether the accused persons are able to dislodge the prosecution's case and rebut the presumption.
14. On the plain reading of the evidence of the father, brother and sister of the deceased, it appears that the deceased was being harassed and the harassment included the physical abuse, not taking her care which includes medical care and forcing her to do household chores despite being pregnant.
17. The judgment in State of West Bengal v. Orilal Jaiswal and anr., : (1994) 1 SCC 73 can be looked into where the following observations were made by the Hon'ble Apex Court:
We are not oblivious that in a criminal trial the degree of proof is stricter than what is required in a civil proceedings.
In a criminal trial however intriguing may be facts and circumstances of the case, the charges made against the accused must be proved beyond all reasonable doubts and the requirement of proof cannot lie in the realm of surmises and conjectures.
The requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not stand altered even after the introduction of section 498A IPC and section 113A of the Indian State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 13 of 29 Evidence Act.
Although, the Court's conscience must be satisfied that the accused is not held guilty when there are reasonable doubts about the complicity of the accused in respect of the offences alleged, it should be borne in mind that there is no absolute standard for proof in a criminal trial and the question whether the charges made against the accused have been proved beyond all reasonable doubts must depend upon the facts and circumstances of the case and the quality of the evidence adduced in the case and the materials placed on record.
27. In this context, reference can be made to the judgment in State of U.P. Vs. Ramesh Kumar Barnwal & Ors. 2008 (1) ACR 818 where it has been observed as follows :
It is very common and probable and Court can take notice of the fact that when there is a mediator through whom marriage has been performed and subsequently shortly after the marriage there is any trouble arising out of the said marriage as in the present case, in the absence of any special reason, parties do approach the mediator for help and the aggrieved party definitely complains him about the conduct of the other side.
Thus, there is every reason than PW3 must have shared of anything was wrong in the relations between Nutan, her husband and other family members.
29.
Her post mortem report reveals the death was due to asphyxia on account of antemortem hanging and the body had no injury indicating that it was her own act.
Accused persons, apparently,
are not at fault if she was not permitted to go.
But then death is a reality which was suicidal in nature.
In these circumstances, can the so called harassment, beatings etc., if at all it was there, is the cause or something else was there.
As regards the aspect of harassment is concerned, the evidence is not such which brings the act of the accused persons into the definition of cruelty and for that matter there is no evidence that the deceased was subjected to any cruelty and cruelty for the purpose of dowry can ,therefore ,not be there either.
31. In these circumstances, the other limb of the arguments raised, with the help of the medical evidence that the victim committed suicide but , in that context, no role is attributable to the accused persons.
It appears that the deceased was not happy with her marriage primarily on account of two reasons that there was a considerable age difference between the deceased and Amod and State Vs. Amod Kumar Mishra and Ors. 23 of 29 Amod was not found good looking by her and is bald.
There are indications that the deceased was either in love or infatuated with somebody else and wanted to get married to him, which could not happen.
Thus, the depression arising out of pregnancy, her unhappiness with the marital alliance was there in suppressed form and the refusal by her husband in taking her for the Kujagra function seems to have triggered a situation where the deceased could not possibly withstood her emotional turmoil and committed suicide.
In these circumstances, when the evidence of dowry related cruelty qua the deceased could not be brought on record, as except in the testimony of the father, sister and brother of the deceased no other witness is there who could have indicated that the deceased was ill treated or harassed and there appears to be no reason or ground to demand a paltry sum of Rs.One Lakh, the accused persons being reasonably well off, the conduct of the father of the deceased in having the attested copy of bill(s) of jewellery readily available with him showing that he came prepared with the intention to lodge a case.
It is not possible that Kashinath Jha would send his son in a primary school at Najafgarh from R.K. Puram.
As such, he could not have been an accused.

All these facts and circumstances put a question mark on the testimony of the father, brother and sister of the deceased and bring the same under cloud and thus makes it untrustworthy.
On the strength of these testimonies it is highly unsafe to record a finding against the accused persons qua their involvement in the offence in any manner.
